name: Cholesterol absorption inhibitors
summary: Cholesterol absorption inhibitors are medicines that lower cholesterol by partly blocking its absorption in the small intestine. They are used on their own when a statin cannot be taken or has not worked, or alongside a statin.
mechanism: Heart UK says ezetimibe partly blocks the absorption of cholesterol in the small intestine. Research reviews describe it as acting on a protein called NPC1L1 in the lining of the small intestine, which helps move cholesterol from the gut into the body. Heart UK says ezetimibe works in a different way from statins, and that the two are often combined because their effects add up.
target: Cholesterol absorption in the small intestine.
classEffects: Stomach pain, diarrhoea, extra wind and tiredness.
With a statin: muscle pain, headaches and moderately raised liver enzymes.
cautions: Unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, or yellowing of the skin or eyes, needs a doctor or NHS 111 straight away, according to the NHS.
The NHS asks people to tell their doctor about pregnancy, planning a pregnancy, breastfeeding and liver problems.
The NHS lists other cholesterol-lowering medicines such as bezafibrate and colestyramine as medicines to mention to a doctor, and UK product information advises caution with ciclosporin.
